lessons.title: Understanding Analogies
lessons.concept: An analogy expresses a relationship between a pair of words/items, and you must find another pair with the same relationship. The key is to identify the exact relationship (e.g., part-whole, cause-effect, tool-user, degree, synonym/antonym, category) in the first pair.
lessons.formula: A : B :: C : ? means A is to B as C is to ?. Identify relation(A,B), apply same to C.
lessons.worked_example: Bird : Nest :: Lion : ? Bird lives in nest; lion lives in den. Answer: Den.
mistakes: Choosing an option merely associated with C but not sharing the same relation
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Common Analogy Relationships
lessons.concept: Common relationships include: part to whole (wheel:car), whole to part, cause to effect (rain:flood), worker to tool (carpenter:hammer), item to category (apple:fruit), degree/intensity (warm:hot), function/purpose, and sequence.
lessons.formula: Test relation explicitly: 'A is a part of B' or 'A is used by B' etc., then verify with C and option.
lessons.worked_example: Pen : Write :: Knife : ? Pen is used to write; knife is used to cut. Relation: tool to function.
mistakes: Confusing similar but different relations (e.g., creator vs user)
Not checking reverse relation when needed
Overlooking multiple possible relations and picking first guess
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Solving Strategy
lessons.concept: Form a clear sentence describing the relationship in the given pair, then apply that exact sentence structure to the second pair. Eliminate options that do not fit. If multiple options seem possible, refine the relationship to be more specific.
lessons.formula: Sentence method: 'A does/has/is ... to B' -> 'C does/has/is ... to ?'
lessons.worked_example: Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ? Doctor works in hospital; teacher works in school. Answer: School.
mistakes: Selecting based on surface similarity only
Ignoring word order in the pair

questions.question: Two options both look plausible for an analogy. What is the correct tie-breaker?

options.A: Choose the first option you like
options.B: Apply the relationship in the SAME direction and degree as the original pair

questions.explanation: Both direction (A:B vs B:A) and degree (exact vs partial similarity) must match. The option preserving both the direction and exactness wins.

questions.question: Odd one out logic is used in analogies when:

options.A: The options form three of one category and one of another

questions.explanation: Sometimes the discrimination works by category: three options share the stem's relationship and one belongs to a different class (or three are of one family and one is not).
